chapter: Harry James, Bellson and the return to Duke
title: Louie Bellson's record date and the Columbia album that never happened
summary: He turned down an album of standards like Stardust, wanting to do his own tunes, and Rose says he was fed up with the business.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Record labels, producers and the business of making albums

blocks.x: Didn't you write something for Louie's first record date?
Yes. On Hobart Boulevard, but I've forgotten what it was now.

Was that Blanche -- no, that was Louie's tune. I remember that it was a 10 inch LP and it was done on Capital -- but I remember Duke and Strayhorn played on the thing and Duke was there at that date. You were there, too, but were you playing? It seems like one of the tunes on Capital was yours.

Well, if Louie played it... and Juan got a contract; they sent Juan a contract on Columbia -- I think it was Columbia -- and told Juan they wanted him to make an album with him; and all at once, I don't know what happened.
No, they wanted for me to do the tune they asked me to do, and I said, 'no, I can't because I don't know anything about those tunes'.
For instance, they wanted me to record

"Stardust" and all those things from way back, and I said, "No, I am not familiar with those kinds of tunes". I wanted to do what I can by myself, or some of my own tunes, but they wouldn't go for that.
That would be great, if you could do an album of your own tunes.

So Juan kind of got disgusted with them. After all, you can't take but so much crap, and it got to look like everybody was trying to put their foot on you and not even give you credit for what you're worth. And I'm not saying this because I'm Juan's wife, but I know Juan is a good musician. He may not know a whole lot about everything else, but he sure knows his music, and he still knows that today. Because you know, once a musician always a musician.
